extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, scholarly-publishing professionals, and academic researchers concerned with peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical observations about how reviewer recruitment difficulty, reviewer behavior, and editorial practices influence manuscript scoring and accept/reject decisions in scholarly journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty recruiting reviewers (measurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recruitment difficulty is measured by the proportion of review invitations that were accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Fox's study this metric (proportion of accepted invitations) was used to quantify how hard editors had to work to obtain reviews for a manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment difficulty predicts editorial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The more difficulty editors had in obtaining reviews on a manuscript, the less likely the manuscript was invited for revision (i.e., ultimately rejected papers experienced more difficulty finding willing reviewers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even after controlling for reviewer assessments, recruitment difficulty still predicted editors’ decisions — suggesting that difficulty itself acts as a signal influencing editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment difficulty predicts manuscript scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts for which editors had less trouble finding reviewers received higher reviewer scores; manuscripts with more trouble received lower scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fox reports a correlation between recruitment ease and reviewer scoring: 'Less trouble: higher scores; more trouble: lower scores.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors may infer negative signal from reviewer declines
rubrics_metrics.description: Declining to review a manuscript may send a subtle message to the editor that the paper is not worth publishing; the more reviewers who decline, the stronger the negative signal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fox postulates editors may be biased against papers for which they have difficulty recruiting reviewers because they over-interpret the recruitment signal or because of annoyance/frustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors' frustration can produce unconscious bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors can become annoyed or frustrated when they must send many invitations to review; this emotional state may produce a residual unconscious bias against the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark Johnston comments editors 'put that frustration aside once the reviews are in hand' but admits editors are human and a small residual unconscious bias is plausible. Fox lacks direct data to test the frustration hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers use title/author/abstract to decide whether to accept
rubrics_metrics.description: Invited reviewers routinely examine title, author, and abstract before committing to review and can often determine from the abstract if the paper is relevant and worth their time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why some manuscripts attract declines quickly: reviewers screen on minimal metadata and may refuse if they judge relevance/importance to be lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desk rejection (editorial screening) as a mitigation tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial rejection (desk rejection) is a key tool: returning papers unlikely to be accepted without external peer review saves editorial effort and reviewer goodwill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tim Vines and other commentators argue editors should probably do more desk rejections to avoid burdening reviewers with low-probability manuscripts and to preserve reviewer goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-profile/selective journals face fewer reviewer recruitment problems
rubrics_metrics.description: High-profile journals that only send out papers that stand a good chance of being published usually do not have trouble recruiting suitable referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By contrast, journals that send many low-probability papers out for review or that have unclear scope may struggle more to find reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals that don't require novelty/significance have more trouble recruiting reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: For journals that do not require manuscripts to report novel or significant findings, locating a willing reviewer may be much more difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This implies scope and acceptance criteria of a journal affect reviewer willingness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial paid independent peer review lacks market acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial options where authors pay to have their paper independently reviewed have failed to gain market acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore, paid independent review is not currently a viable widespread solution to reviewer scarcity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-suggested reviewers as a practical mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors can ask authors to suggest names of potential reviewers and then vet that list to help fill reviewer slots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several commentators note asking authors for reviewer suggestions is a pragmatic approach when editors struggle to secure reviewers, though caution and vetting are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial systems and editor training affect reviewer discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Many reviewer-database entries go unused because associate editors don't fully learn how to find reviewers in the system or default to searching by names they know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training editors in database search functions can produce 'aha' moments and expand the pool of candidates beyond familiar names.

rubrics_metrics.name: No good mechanism for volunteers to signal reviewer availability
rubrics_metrics.description: There is often no easy way for a willing party to meaningfully signal interest to be a reviewer beyond creating a generic reviewer account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors report receiving volunteers at conferences but lack efficient ways to surface or prioritize these volunteers in selection workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement problems with policies requiring authors to review
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals have policies that accepted authors must complete at least one review in the following year, but tracking and enforcing such policies is difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if such policies exist, resource constraints make enforcement challenging, limiting their effectiveness in increasing reviewer supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expand reviewer pool via diversity and analytic tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Expanding the reviewer pool by looking beyond traditional networks (geography, demographics) and using tools to identify suitable reviewers can increase speed and accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters suggest embracing diversity/inclusion and implementing reviewer-identification/analytic tools to broaden and improve reviewer selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty finding reviewers can disproportionately penalize outlier/novel work
rubrics_metrics.description: Work that is out of the mainstream or highly novel may struggle to find reviewers and thus be disadvantaged by recruitment-based signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters reference historical and anecdotal cases where novel ideas were penalized because few in the community were willing or able to review them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated rejections of reviewer invitations can lead to less-qualified reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: As an editor sends out a manuscript repeatedly, later candidate reviewers may be farther from the paper’s core competence, producing less informed reviews; editors may give greater weight to a negative recommendation from such reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dynamic can compound problems: poor fit reviewers give thin negative recommendations and editors may treat such negatives as decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial scope and focus influence reviewer recruitment success
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of a journal and its editorial team composition affect the ability to recruit reviewers; refocusing scope may mitigate recruitment issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters ask whether editorial team scope or journal iteration contributes to reviewer difficulty and suggest authors consider journal scope before submitting.
